title: External outage chronicle and technical safeguards brief
content:
Purpose and audience:
This is a customer-facing draft that combines a concise status-page update format with a longer post-incident chronicle and technical safeguards summary. Intended recipients: account owners, SRE contacts, and technical product leads at impacted customers.

Document goals:
- Provide a short, clear status page blurb customers can post to their teams immediately.
- Offer a longer chronological timeline and technical explanation suitable for customers who require forensic detail.
- Describe mitigations we applied in real time and durable safeguards we will implement to reduce recurrence risk.
- Template section for customer-facing follow-up (compensation/credit language, SLA implications).

Quick status (1-2 sentence status-page blurb) — short form for 1st update:
- Incident started: 2026-08-08 14:22 UTC. Impact: multi-region elevated latency and transient request failures for text-generation endpoints.
- Current status: degradation mitigations in place; partial recovery observed in US-east and EU-west; APAC region traffic is routed to fallback pools. Investigations ongoing; no data loss.

Expanded status page update (for next update cycle, ~30–60 min):
- Timeline summary: 14:22 UTC — large spike in request queue depth on serving-runtime due to malformed traffic pattern (high concurrency of long-context streamed requests). 14:30 UTC — autoscaler mis-evaluated burst mode and attempted aggressive rebalancing; 14:36 UTC — KV-cache thrashing observed leading to increased per-token latency and request failures. 14:45 UTC — implemented temporary rate-limiter on streaming endpoints and increased conservative autoscaler caps; 15:05 UTC — partial recovery begins; 15:40 UTC — routing rules applied to drain overloaded pools and move traffic to pre-warmed fallback nodes.
- User impact: up to 40% of requests experienced >5s latency or 5xx errors during peak window. Customers using long-context streaming (>=8k tokens) were disproportionately affected.
- Customer action: no customer-side action required. If you rely on strict latency SLOs, consider switching to the non-streaming short-context endpoints (instructions link).

Technical chronicle (detailed, for technical customers):
- Observed metrics: request queue depth 3x baseline; KV cache miss rate rose from 2% to 46%; GPU utilization uneven (some nodes at 98%, others idle), tail latency P99 jumped from 0.9s to 7.4s.
- Root-cause hypothesis (working): a sudden burst of malformed stream init messages (a client-side bug in a partner integration) generated a large number of half-open streaming sessions. The runtime batch planner assumed many of these were active tokens requiring KV cache population, leading to excessive KV eviction and cache thrash. Simultaneously, autoscaler logic mis-classified the pattern as short-lived burst and attempted to rebalance by moving model shards between nodes, which amplified cache misses.
- Why fallback safeguards didn’t fully stop the impact: the fallback model variants were compatible but not pre-warmed for the specific long-context streaming pattern, so while routing mitigated some failures, the mismatch in pre-warmed cache state caused higher latency until fallback instances warmed.

Mitigations applied during the incident (real-time):
- Immediate: enabled temporary heuristic-based rate-limiter for streaming endpoint (reduced malformed session inflow).
- Rebalance: disabled aggressive shard-rebalance behavior in the autoscaler for the affected pools.
- Routing: manually routed new connections to pre-warmed fallback pools and increased concurrency limits there.
- Monitoring: added short-lived alert to tracking dashboards for KV-cache miss rate >30%.

Planned durable safeguards (post-incident roadmap items):
- Autoscaler policy changes: add burst-detection gating to prevent shard moves during unknown short-lived spikes; conservative default for streaming endpoints. (ETA: 3 weeks)
- Pre-warm logic improvement: extend pre-warm heuristics to consider long-context streaming patterns and maintain a small standing pool of pre-warmed fallback instances per region. (ETA: 4–6 weeks)
- KV-cache priority: introduce eviction safeguards and shard-local sticky caches for streaming sessions to reduce global cache churn. (ETA: 6–8 weeks)
- Traffic filtering: develop outbound client-side input validation guidance and defensive parsing at the edge to discard malformed session inits earlier. (ETA: 2 weeks for guidance, 8–10 weeks for edge enforcement)

Customer-facing postmortem summary (concise):
- What happened: a burst of malformed streaming session starts caused our serving runtime to thrash KV cache and the autoscaler to rebalance shards aggressively, producing elevated latency and request failures across multiple regions.
- Impact: transient latency >5s and occasional 5xx errors for a subset of text-generation streaming requests; no persisted user data was lost and all requests that completed returned valid responses.
- Root cause: interaction between malformed client behavior and autoscaler/shard-rebalance heuristics exposing a gap in pre-warm assumptions for long-context streaming.
- What we did: applied emergency rate-limits, disabled aggressive rebalancing, routed traffic to warmed fallback pools; restored service to normal within ~1 hour.
- What we will do: implement autoscaler and pre-warm improvements, add cache eviction protections, and deliver improved edge validation. Expected timeline: 2–10 weeks depending on item.

Recommended customer update templates:
- Short email/SMS blurb (for account teams):
  Subject: [Redwood] Recent latency incident — quick summary and next steps
  Body: We experienced a transient latency and error spike on text-generation streaming endpoints on 2026-08-08. The majority of traffic was restored within one hour. We have implemented mitigations and are rolling out changes to reduce recurrence risk; no customer data was lost. We'll follow up with a short postmortem and timeline.

- Longer customer email (for customers requesting detail):
  Subject: Post-incident summary: streaming latency incident (2026-08-08)
  Body: Includes expanded timeline, technical chronicle, impacted endpoints, and planned mitigations (paste the "Customer-facing postmortem summary" section). Offer a scheduled call with their SRE/Account lead.

SLA and credits guidance (customer success note):
- Preliminary: Incident severity qualifies as Severity 2 for affected customers under current SLA language because of sustained elevated errors and latency. Work with Finance/Sales for any credit calculations; include usage window and impacted token/time weighting.
- Suggested phrasing: "We will assess SLA credits for impacted customers; account teams will reach out with next steps by XX date."

FAQ (for CS + support teams to use in replies):
- Q: Was customer data affected? A: No. We have verified there was no persisted data loss.
- Q: Do I need to take action? A: No action required; we will notify you if any config changes are recommended.
- Q: Is this related to model weights or privacy? A: No — this was an infrastructure/serving incident not related to model parameters or data handling.

Open questions / internal follow-ups (notes to engineers & incident lead):
- Confirm origin of malformed stream inits — partner integration vs. internal SDK bug (investigation ticket: INC-4321).
- Validate fallback pre-warm sizing per region (owner: Diego).
- Quantify affected customer list and compute candidate credit amounts (owner: Lina / Sales ops).
- Create a short KB for customers describing best practices for streaming (owner: Omar).

Proposed timeline for customer communications:
- t+0 (immediate): short status page blurb (use "Quick status" above).
- t+1h: expanded status page with timeline and initial mitigations.
- t+72h: draft postmortem delivered to impacted customers, invite for technical call.
- t+14d: follow-up showing roadmap items and ETA for safeguards.

Draft sign-off checklist for external postmortem:
- Incident lead sign-off (Maya)
- SRE validation of metrics and root-cause wording (Diego)
- Product engineering sign-off on planned mitigations and ETA (Lina)
- Legal review if any customer contracts require special language (placeholder)

Notes to self (informal):
- Keep language non-technical in the short blurb; avoid internal process details.
- Be explicit about "no data loss" early in every customer-facing message.
- If customers ask about credits, route to AC/Finance and include a private spreadsheet with affected windows (do NOT share publicly).

Version history:
- 2026-08-09: initial draft (Maya)
- 2026-08-12: added expanded timeline and initial mitigations (Diego)
- 2026-08-20: updated planned safeguards and communication timeline (Lina)

Attachments / useful links (paste into outgoing customer mail where appropriate):
- Internal incident page: https://confluence.example.com/ops/incident-4321
- Public status page: https://status.redwood.ai
- Support scheduling link: https://calendly.com/redwood/incident-review

End of draft.

---
Internal quick checklist for publishing on status.redwood.ai:
- [ ] Grab short blurb from "Quick status"
- [ ] Add impacted regions and affected endpoints list
- [ ] Link to full customer postmortem once reviewed
- [ ] Flag account teams for high-touch customers
- [ ] Schedule follow-up message at t+72h

Unresolved: whether to proactively offer a one-time account credit vs. wait for customer-initiated requests — recommend Finance ops guidance before public announcement.
